# What is reproducible science?

Reproducibility is not one tool or a final checkbox. It is a way of organizing research so that evidence can be traced from the original inputs, through documented decisions and code, to the reported result.

This chapter introduces the distinction between reproducibility and replication, explains why transparent workflows benefit both authors and readers, and connects those practices to the FAIR principles.

## Activity: Thought Exercise

- What does reproducible science mean to you?
- Which tools have you previously used?
- Which tools are you most excited to learn?

Keep your answers nearby as you work through the course. Revisit them at the end and identify which parts of your definition became more concrete.

## What is reproducible science?

Reproducible science makes the research process transparent to the greatest extent permitted by ethics, law, consent, and funding agreements. Transparency does not mean publishing sensitive data without safeguards; it means documenting what can be shared and explaining restrictions on what cannot.

  - Sharing experiment and analysis code
  - Detailed methods sections
  - Sharing stimulus sets
  - Being able to walk through a data analysis start (load raw data) to finish (manuscript analyses) in code
  - Following FAIR Principles
  - Pre-registering hypotheses and analysis plans (e.g., on OSF)

### Benefits of Reproducible Research

Sourced from: [https://www.displayr.com/what-is-reproducible-research](https://www.displayr.com/what-is-reproducible-research 
)

  - increased likelihood that the research will be correct
  - reproducibility makes it easier to check the research
  - it is easier to reproduce the research independently
  - easier to extend the research
  - reusable code and instruction resulting in increased efficiencies

These benefits also apply within a research team. A well-documented project makes handoffs, error checking, future analyses, and manuscript revisions less dependent on one person's memory.
  
### Reproducible vs Replicable

  - Reproducible: when the exact results can be reproduced if given access to the original data, software, or code
  - Replicable: research results can be reproduced by independent researchers using different methods.

The terms are sometimes used differently across fields, so define them when writing for a broad audience. In this course, reproducibility means obtaining the same results from the same materials, while replication asks whether the finding persists in a new study.

## FAIR Principles

FAIR describes properties that help data and related research objects remain useful over time. FAIR does not automatically mean fully open: access can be controlled while metadata, formats, and reuse conditions remain clear.

  - ***F: Findable***: "The first step in (re)using data is to find them. Metadata and data should be easy to find for both humans and computers. Machine-readable metadata are essential for automatic discovery of datasets and services"
  - ***A: Accessible***: "Once the user finds the required data, she/he/they need to know how they can be accessed, possibly including authentication and authorisation."
  - ***I: Interoperable***: "The data usually need to be integrated with other data. In addition, the data need to interoperate with applications or workflows for analysis, storage, and processing."
  - ***R: Reusable***: "The ultimate goal of FAIR is to optimise the reuse of data. To achieve this, metadata and data should be well-described so that they can be replicated and/or combined in different settings."

  - [Learn more about the FAIR Principles](https://www.go-fair.org/fair-principles/)
  - [FAIR Principles Info PDF](https://www.go-fair.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/01/FAIRPrinciples_overview.pdf)

## Takeaways

A reproducible workflow connects transparency, documentation, code, versioned materials, and clear access conditions. The goal is not perfection; it is to make the path from evidence to claim easier to inspect, repeat, and extend.
